summary: Catalytic cores of soluble metabolic enzymes centered on carboxylation/carboxyl-transfer and nucleotide-cofactor–mediated group-transfer chemistries across all domains of life; includes ATP-dependent biotin carboxylase and ATP-independent carboxyltransferase modules, plus Rossmann/GT-B/PurM/class II aaRS folds that bind ATP, FAD/NAD, or nucleotide-sugars
activation_pattern: Domain-level activation over long internal, contiguous stretches (often mid-sequence ~300–500 aa), sometimes with a second segment in multidomain enzymes; residues enriched for polar/charged/small side chains typical of phosphate/dinucleotide-binding loops and catalytic networks

summary: NTP-dependent small-molecule kinase module (phosphotransferase core) centered on the guanylate-kinase–like/nucleoside monophosphate (NMP) kinase family and extending to closely related kinase folds (e.g., APS kinase, dephospho-CoA kinase, shikimate kinase, and uridine/deoxycytidine kinases), including catalytically inactive GK-like domains in MAGUKs.
activation_pattern: Domain-level, typically a long contiguous block across the kinase module, spanning glycine-rich/basic segments and the phosphate-binding loop (P-loop/Walker or equivalent), into the core β-sheet and lid/C-terminal helices; strongest peaks often occur in the lid/C-terminal helix and persist in pseudoenzymes.

summary: Residues at or immediately preceding the N-termini of alpha-helices (helix N-cap/helix-start positions), often appearing as short di-/tripeptides enriched for helix-initiating/capping residues (D/E/S/T/N, sometimes P just before the helix, and A/L/V/K/R at the first helical turn); a secondary-structure boundary motif rather than a specific functional site, seen across soluble and membrane proteins
activation_pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated at helix starts, frequently as 1–3 contiguous residues; occasionally extends across short acidic runs at successive helix onsets; occurs within well-structured regions and typically does not coincide with annotated catalytic residues

summary: Phospho-regulated, Ser/Thr/Pro–rich intrinsically disordered or coiled-coil terminal scaffolds of eukaryotic complex‑assembly proteins, spanning chromosome segregation (HORMA/kinetochore/cohesin/condensin), autophagy initiation PI3K complexes, microtubule nucleation (Augmin/HAUS and gamma‑TuRC adaptors), SPX/EXS phosphate‑homeostasis systems, vesicle tethering (exocyst), transcriptional Mediator submodules, and selected microtubule‑associated transport adaptors (e.g., IFT/CLUAP1).
activation_pattern: Regional activation over terminal low‑complexity segments (often N‑terminal but also C‑terminal), tens to hundreds of residues, enriched in Ser/Thr (often S/T‑P) and simple repeats; frequently disordered and/or coiled; limited activation within adjacent folded domains (e.g., HORMA, SPX), with allowance for short regulatory loops/tails (e.g., Mad2 safety‑belt).

summary: Cysteine-dependent phosphatase catalytic core of the protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) fold, recognizing the conserved active-site architecture (HCX5R P-loop and WPD/WPE general-acid loop) across classical receptor and non-receptor PTPs, dual-specificity PTPs, and PTP-fold lipid phosphatases (PTEN, myotubularins), including bacterial secreted PTP effectors and inactive/pseudo-PTPs.
activation_pattern: Domain-level activation over long contiguous segments corresponding to the cytosolic PTP catalytic domain (often near the C-terminus in receptor-type PTPs), with strong residue-level peaks at the WPD/WPE loop and the catalytic Cys/Arg P-loop (HCX5R), and secondary signal over adjacent pTyr-recognition/Q-loops; inactive homologs still activate. Off-target, weaker, and less contiguous activation can occur in other hydrolases.

summary: Core register positions within helices of long alpha-helical scaffolds—especially HEAT/ARM alpha‑solenoid repeats and closely related helical repeat arrays—and, more sparsely, isolated stable helices embedded in other folds (e.g., alpha/beta enzymes or tether heads); the signal prefers well‑folded alpha‑helical segments and is depleted in disordered regions and most beta‑strand cores.
activation_pattern: Residue‑level peaks that recur periodically across tandem repeats (often ~one per HEAT/ARM unit) and, when repeats are absent, appear as sparse peaks on isolated, high‑confidence helices within larger domains; little to no activation in flexible/disordered linkers, low‑pLDDT segments, signal peptides, or beta‑sheet cores.

summary: A generic transmembrane-helix signature of 12‑TM secondary carrier transporters (MFS and closely related SLC-like families), capturing the membrane-embedded alpha-helical segments that form the transport core rather than substrate- or loop-specific motifs; prefers hydrophobic/aromatic and small residues (G/A/S/T) and avoids charged residues.
activation_pattern: Regional activation confined to multiple transmembrane alpha-helices across the protein, with discrete residue-level peaks within those helices; little to no activation in cytoplasmic/extracellular loops or termini.

summary: Generic alpha-helical secondary-structure signal: the feature highlights well-ordered, amphipathic alpha-helices within globular domains, an element frequently used in RNA-associated proteins (e.g., dsRNA-binding motifs and RNA helicases) but broadly present across diverse enzyme and membrane-associated proteins
activation_pattern: Residue-level peaks that cluster within short stretches of alpha-helix; multiple scattered sites per protein proportional to helical content; preference for hydrophobic/aromatic residues with some charged positions; typically away from annotated catalytic or metal-binding residues and instead marking structural helical segments with high confidence

summary: Acidic donor–diphosphate engagement hotspot in glycosyltransferases and nucleotidyltransferases that stabilizes the NDP/NTP and any required metal. This is most often a short acidic cluster (e.g., DxD/TED in GT-A), but can be noncanonical acidic pairs in GT-B (often metal-independent) or His/acidic ligands (e.g., HxH with adjacent Asp/Glu) in polβ-like nucleotidyltransferases. The feature spans processive polysaccharide synthases, secretory/lipid glycosyltransferases, and diverse nucleotidyltransferases across all domains of life.
activation_pattern: Residue-level peaks on short 3–5 residue acidic-rich windows within donor-binding/catalytic loops; processive polymerases may show multiple nearby acidic sites. Variants include His-containing metal ligands when flanked by acidic residues (NTase folds).

summary: Short acidic–aromatic low‑complexity motifs: D/E‑rich stretches containing di‑aromatic pairs (especially YY, also FF/WW) in exposed loops or terminal regions, acting as generic short linear patches present across many protein families and taxa
activation_pattern: Regional activation on short windows (~8–30 aa) with sharp peaks over consecutive aromatics (YY/FF/WW) and interspersed acidic residues; commonly located near N‑termini in bacteria/fungi and in regulatory C‑terminal segments in eukaryotes; multiple clustered windows can occur within a local region

summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity N‑terminal extensions of AAA+/P‑loop NTPases that precede the structured catalytic core; typically enriched for mixed basic/acidic residues and helical propensity but low confidence, serving as flexible interaction/regulatory tails rather than the Walker A/B motifs
activation_pattern: Regional activation confined to the extreme N‑terminus (roughly the first 20–250 residues), often with multiple peaks within the disordered segment; activation drops to near zero upon entering the folded AAA+ domain and is absent at annotated ATP‑binding (Walker) sites

summary: Active-site–adjacent, His/Asp/Glu–enriched structural segments that form or flank metal-binding and acid/base networks in enzyme catalytic cores—most prominently the Zn- or Cu-cofactor environments of metalloenzymes (metallopeptidases, multicopper oxidases), but more broadly analogous substrate‑binding groove scaffolds in diverse hydrolases and RNA‑modifying enzymes.
activation_pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous stretches within catalytic domains (mixed beta/alpha/coil), often abutting or partially overlapping annotated metal-binding histidines/glutamates; peaks tend to sit on neighboring residues rather than the canonical motif residues themselves. Frequently appears in multiple regions of the same protein. Little to no activation on signal peptides or distal propeptides.

summary: Structured mid-domain segments that build the active-site/substrate or prosthetic-cofactor binding neighborhood of enzyme catalytic cores, i.e., regions flanking catalytic residues or embedding redox/cofactor ligation motifs within the catalytic domain
activation_pattern: Regional activation in long, contiguous blocks in the central portion of proteins; mixed secondary structure; high structural confidence; local peaks at or immediately adjacent to catalytic residues or cofactor-ligating motifs; little to no signal in signal peptides, propeptides, or terminal/linker regions

summary: Recognition helix of helix–turn–helix DNA-binding domains: the feature primarily marks the basic, major-groove–contacting alpha helix (and immediately adjacent turn/helix) in HTH-type transcription factors across bacteria and eukaryotes (LuxR-type regulators, two‑component response regulators, ECF sigma factor domain-4, and homeobox/homeodomain proteins); outside these contexts it occasionally fires weakly on isolated residues in stable secondary-structure elements with similar physicochemical character
activation_pattern: Domain-/regional activation in canonical cases: contiguous 20–40 aa windows centered on the HTH motif with strongest signal on the second (recognition) helix, often in C‑terminal DNA-binding regions of bacterial regulators; sparse, single-residue peaks in unrelated proteins, typically within well-ordered helices (rarely other secondary structure) without clear DNA-binding function

summary: EF-hand Ca2+-binding helix–loop–helix modules (canonical and pseudo EF-hands) in calmodulin-like domains, including penta‑EF‑hand families; the feature targets the acidic 12‑residue Ca2+-coordinating loop and adjacent helices repeated in Ca2+ sensors/regulators across eukaryotes, including regulatory EF-hand inserts of enzymes, channels, ciliary proteins, and some secreted EF-hand proteins, and also certain EF-hand-like acidic Ca2+-binding segments in ER/secretory luminal regions.
activation_pattern: Repeated short regional activations with sharp residue-level peaks at Asp/Glu (and Gly) positions of the 12-residue EF-hand loop; clusters recur every ~25–35 residues corresponding to EF-hand repeats; in multidomain proteins, activation is confined to the EF-hand module(s) (often specifically at the N- or C-terminus depending on the family), yielding long activation lists when many EF-hands are present; occasionally detects short acidic luminal segments lacking the full helix–loop–helix context.

summary: Short alpha-helix boundary/capping segments—often juxtamembrane or at the N-terminus of the mature chain—enriched in small/polar residues (Ser/Thr/Ala, sometimes Pro) with nearby basic residues, including helix‑breaking Gly/Pro in interhelical linkers; marks flexible helix–coil transitions when the local sequence is low-complexity and poorly ordered (not universal across families).
activation_pattern: Regional activation on short 3–10 residue patches at helix–coil junctions; occasional single-residue peaks at hinge Gly; preferentially just cytosolic to transmembrane helices or early N-terminal segments after signal peptide when those segments are S/T/A-rich and low-complexity; often absent in well-ordered or glycosylation-dense luminal regions; sporadic and not conserved across all orthologs within soluble domains.

summary: A generic structural signal for well-ordered alpha-helical surface patches (often amphipathic), frequently in C-terminal segments; typically adjacent to, or part of, interaction- or ligand-proximal helices rather than catalytic residues, consistent with mixed charged and small/hydrophobic residues.
activation_pattern: Residue-level peaks clustered on one or two alpha-helices within high-confidence structured regions; ~5–15 residues per protein; strong avoidance of disordered regions and beta strands; frequent bias toward C-terminal helices; peaks often lie near (but not exactly on) annotated ligand-, nucleic acid-, or protein-interaction and PTM sites.

summary: A charged, amphipathic alpha‑helical module (often a helix–loop–helix segment) used as a packing/interface helix within enzyme cores and inter‑domain linkers; frequently positioned mid‑chain and sometimes bordering cofactor/nucleotide pockets, but not marking catalytic residues themselves.
activation_pattern: Regional activation over a contiguous 40–120 aa block centered on one or more alpha‑helices plus adjacent loops; strongest on helical cores and neighboring coil turns; typically mid‑chain and occasionally spanning flexible inter‑domain linkers; minor secondary peaks can occur elsewhere.

summary: Residue‑level “micro‑hotspots” composed of small/polar (S/T/G/A) or acidic (D/E) side chains—and occasionally a single aliphatic residue—at tightly packed, functionally constrained positions; in membrane receptors this often corresponds to a polar/branched site within a transmembrane helix (helix‑packing/kink or interaction spot) or a short extracellular/periplasmic patch, while in soluble enzymes it coincides with catalytic/ligand‑binding acidic or small residues
activation_pattern: Predominantly residue‑level peaks (1–2 residues), sometimes short 3–10 aa patches; typically mid‑chain. Frequently inside a single transmembrane helix (central polar/branched pair) or in extracellular/periplasmic segments of receptors; in soluble enzymes, at conserved catalytic/ligand‑coordinating acidic/small residues. Rarely extends over longer stretches.

summary: Short amphipathic alpha‑helical coupling elements at transmembrane boundaries—juxtamembrane helices, S4–S5–type linkers, and gly/pro‑containing hinge positions—that transmit conformational changes between membrane‑embedded helices and cytosolic/periplasmic modules in channels and secondary transporters; analogous short helices in soluble enzymes are weakly captured.
activation_pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered over short (≈5–20 aa) alpha‑helical stretches, typically immediately before or after a transmembrane helix, with occasional peaks inside TM helices at kink/hinge residues; enriched for mixed charged/polar and small/hydrophobic residues (frequent G and P). Coverage is sparse and discontinuous across a protein; targeting signal peptides show little/no activation.

summary: Recognition of low‑complexity, glycine/proline/serine–enriched intrinsically disordered segments—especially long prion‑like domains, flexible head/tail regions of cytoskeletal proteins, and juxta‑membrane cytosolic/luminal tails with Gly clusters, Pro tracts, and frequent aromatic‑Gly patterns—with a minor secondary signal for the conserved catalytic Aspartate in TruA‑family pseudouridine synthases.
activation_pattern: Primarily regional/domain‑level activation across long, compositionally biased IDRs that begin where structural confidence drops and fade at the onset of well‑structured helices/coiled‑coils or within stable domains; enrichment for G/P/S, Gly clusters, and Pro‑rich stretches. Minimal activation in folded domains. Occasional single‑residue peaks at conserved catalytic Asp in TruA enzymes.

summary: A short, conserved alpha-helical patch in the ABC ATPase nucleotide-binding domain that forms the NBD–TMD coupling interface (adjacent to the signature/C-loop LSGGQ and the Q/H/D-loop “switch” region), rather than the catalytic Walker A/B sites.
activation_pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks confined to a narrow helix or helix–coil boundary within the cytosolic ABC transporter (NBD) domain; one hotspot per NBD (two in full-length eukaryotic ABCs: mid-sequence and near the C-terminus). In bacterial soluble ABC ATPases, peaks cluster around positions ~90–120 of the NBD. Little to no signal on the P-loop/ATP-binding residues or transmembrane helices. Activated residues are predominantly hydrophobic (I/L/V/M) with frequent G and basic (K/R), often accompanied by E/D and occasional P, consistent with a conserved, surface-exposed coupling helix/kink.

summary: Structural helix-adjacent loops and short alpha-helical linkers that scaffold large soluble proteins—especially alpha-rich repeat/barrel folds—rather than catalytic or ligand-binding sites; commonly seen in extracellular CAZymes and secreted glycoproteins, and in helical-repeat enzymes (prenyltransferase β)
activation_pattern: Regional activation across multiple short-to-medium stretches within a domain, with peaks at coil-to-helix transitions and loops connecting helices/repeats; often clustered in C-terminal alpha-rich blocks in CAZymes; frequently enriched in D/E, G, and hydrophobic/aromatic residues; generally away from annotated active or binding sites; includes disulfide-bonded loop segments in secreted proteins

summary: Generic β-strand/β-sheet core signal: the feature activates on well-ordered β-strands and their flanking turns that form the sheet cores of ubiquitous α/β enzyme folds (e.g., TIM barrel, Rossmann/GT‑B, enolase/IlvD-like, and related), rather than on catalytic motifs or specific cofactors
activation_pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in DSSP E segments and adjacent tight turns across long regions of the catalytic domain; low signal in helices and disordered tails. Activated residues are enriched for small/hydrophobic (G/A/V/L/I) with S/T, with occasional acidic/His in loop/turn positions. Broad regional activation across multiple β-strands instead of at single catalytic residues; typically falls within the mature folded domain rather than signal/transit peptides

summary: Flavin (FAD/FMN) cofactor–binding core of flavoprotein oxidoreductases: the Rossmann-like FAD-binding domain encompassing the glycine-rich phosphate-binding loop(s) and adjacent aromatic (often Trp) elements that cradle the isoalloxazine ring, shared across FAD-dependent amine oxidases, monooxygenases/halogenases, and protoporphyrinogen oxidases; with rare cross-activation of glycine/Trp-rich internal segments in non-flavin enzymes (e.g., some membrane isoprenoid cyclases) that mimic these sequence features; occasional cross-activation of similar Rossmann segments in non-flavin dehydrogenases
activation_pattern: Primarily domain-level activation over medium-to-long contiguous stretches spanning the FAD-binding Rossmann core (glycine- and Gly–Pro–rich loops with nearby Trp), typically in internal or C‑terminal regions; occasional activation on analogous glycine-rich internal stretches in non-flavin proteins; not dependent on cellular localization

summary: The canonical J-domain HPD catalytic loop and its flanking helix–turn segment that engages Hsp70 and stimulates ATP hydrolysis (the helix II–III HPD loop of Hsp40/DnaJ and J-like domains), recognized across eukaryotic, bacterial, and viral proteins.
activation_pattern: Compact, contiguous activation within annotated J domains (typically 15–40 residues), rising along the preceding helix and peaking precisely at the His–Pro–Asp (HPD) tripeptide in the helix-to-coil loop, with tapering into immediate neighbors; often accompanied by basic (Lys/Arg) flanks and occasional Lys or Gly–Gly immediately after HPD; essentially silent outside J domains, with only rare low-level hits from short HPD-like matches in unrelated proteins.

summary: Short β-strand/turn micro‑motifs at β‑sheet edges—loop→β‑strand junctions enriched in Gly/Ser/Thr with small hydrophobics and often a Ser/Thr “cap,” sometimes accompanied by basic residues. Frequently manifests as a conserved short G–[I/V]–T–like segment within β‑rich cytosolic domains, but occurs broadly across folds and functions.
activation_pattern: Localized short windows (≈5–15 aa) with sharp residue‑level peaks centered on the start or middle of a short β‑strand or the immediately preceding/following loop; multiple independent windows can appear across large or multi‑pass proteins; occurs in both soluble domains and cytosolic loops of membrane proteins.

summary: Low-complexity, Pro/Ser/Thr- and charge-rich linker/hinge segments at domain boundaries—typically non‑hydrophobic stretches marking coil↔helix transitions, first β‑strands or domain‑to‑disorder junctions—connecting or flanking structured domains in large, multi‑domain proteins; emphasized in secreted/luminal loops and cytosolic tails as well as regulatory linkers in transcription factors and bacterial envelope enzymes, rather than catalytic or DNA‑binding cores.
activation_pattern: Regional activation in contiguous runs; strongest at boundary transitions (coil-to-helix starts, first β‑strand/turn motifs, domain-to-disorder edges); little/no signal in transmembrane helices, catalytic residues, or well‑packed domain cores. Prefers non‑hydrophobic segments enriched for P/S/T/Gly and charged residues with frequent SP/TP/PP dipeptides; often low pLDDT except when highlighting the first ordered β‑edge of a domain.

summary: Generic feature, meaning not known

Flexible glycine-rich, low-complexity coil/linker segments exposed to the extracellular/periplasmic environment—most prominently the long surface loops of Gram-negative outer-membrane β-barrels (porins/secretins, autotransporters/ushers) and other secreted proteins—often containing short small/polar motifs (GxG, TGG, DTG, GP) and avoiding well-structured cores.
activation_pattern: Predominantly long, contiguous activation blocks across low-pLDDT coil/disordered regions; minimal-to-absent signal in β-strands/α-helices of structured domains; sharp residue-level peaks at glycine/small-residue motifs (e.g., GxG/DTG) within these flexible segments; cytosolic proteins show only short localized patches at such motifs.

summary: Adenosine-nucleotide cofactor–binding segment: a glycine-rich, Rossmann-like β–α–β region that contacts NAD(H)/NADP(H), with generalization to analogous ATP/adenylate-binding loops in adenylate-forming (E1-like) enzymes; the feature highlights the cofactor-binding lobe rather than catalytic residues.
activation_pattern: Regional activation over long contiguous stretches (~60–100 aa), usually in mid-protein (sometimes N-terminal in Rossmann folds), spanning β-strands, α-helices, and flexible glycine-rich loops; residue-level peaks often occur on Gly/Ser/Thr and nearby Lys/Arg that engage phosphate groups; activation frequently overlaps annotated NAD(P)+ or ATP-binding residues and can peak in low‑pLDDT loops that close over the cofactor.

summary: Activation segment of protein kinases (the DFG-to-APE/Y-PE region), encompassing the activation loop and adjoining P+1 loop within the conserved kinase catalytic core across Ser/Thr, tyrosine, and dual-specificity kinases, including eukaryote-like bacterial and viral kinases.
activation_pattern: Regional activation: a single 20–40 aa stretch inside the kinase domain that starts at or just after the DFG motif and extends toward the conserved APE/Y-PE anchor. Peaks are strongest immediately C-terminal to DFG within the flexible activation loop and often near the terminal PE motif; other catalytic elements (e.g., glycine-rich loop, catalytic Asp) are largely ignored. Occasionally appears as two close blocks corresponding to subsegments of the activation/P+1 loop. The region is frequently conformationally flexible/low-confidence in structure predictions.
